short: An English naval administrator whose meticulously kept private diary provides a primary source for major events of the Restoration period.
full:
Samuel Pepys was an English naval administrator and Member of Parliament who rose to become Chief Secretary to the Admiralty under both Charles II and James II. Despite lacking early maritime experience, his administrative reforms, emphasis on professionalisation, and logistical acumen laid the foundations for the modern Royal Navy. However, he is best remembered today not for his official career, but for the private diary he kept for nearly a decade between 1660 and 1669.

Written in shorthand and rarely self-censoring, Pepys's diary offers an extraordinarily vivid, candid, and personal account of daily life in seventeenth-century London. He recorded both his private indiscretions and his firsthand observations of some of the era's most defining historical events, including the restoration of the monarchy, the ravages of the Great Plague of 1665, and the devastating Great Fire of London in 1666. The manuscript was bequeathed to Magdalene College, Cambridge, and remained unpublished until the nineteenth century, when it became a cornerstone of English historical literature.
